messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Minh Tran was 72 when he came to treatment, a married South Eastern Asian man who had spent most of his working life helping other displaced families find food, shelter, and paperwork in the wake of violence. He had survived the bombing of a relief convoy years earlier, an attack that still came back to him not as a full story but as fragments: the flash of light at the roadside, the crumpled metal of the truck, the dust hanging in the air, the faces of people he had been speaking with only seconds before. When he tried to describe it, he would often stop and say it seemed hard to believe it had happened to him at all, as if the scene belonged to someone else’s life. What remained most vividly were pictures and images, and sometimes, when the memory surfaced, he would hear the same sounds in his head that had cut through the explosion—sirens, shouting, the high, metallic ringing that followed the blast.

Those fragments were enough to keep Minh turning the event over and over in his mind. Because the memory felt so extreme and unreal, he kept searching it for what he had done wrong, repeatedly blaming himself for not noticing danger sooner, for continuing down the route, for failing the people who had trusted him to get them through safely. The more he replayed it, the more certain he became that ordinary life could turn suddenly catastrophic. He was increasingly watchful in a way his wife recognized immediately: scanning entrances, watching the road before crossing, sitting where he could see people coming and going. Over time, he came to believe that safety existed only in a very small number of places—his home, a particular corner of the living room, the quiet back seat of his own house—not in the wider world where he once moved so freely.

That sense of danger narrowed his life. Driving, once an ordinary part of his work and errands, became intolerable; he stopped getting behind the wheel and avoided being a passenger whenever he could, because the sound and movement of vehicles brought back the blast before he could brace himself. He also began steering away from any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation. At the aid office, he would stay silent in meetings where he might otherwise have spoken plainly, and at home he would smooth over small conflicts rather than risk raised voices or tension. He told himself that keeping peace was safer than standing his ground, and the effort to stay guarded made his days smaller and more tense.

The narrowness of his safe places only deepened his vigilance. In the market, a dropped pan or a motorcycle backfiring would make him jump. In the aid center, a slammed file drawer or a sudden laugh in the hallway could send a sharp jolt through him, and he would look up immediately, already searching for what might happen next. The sounds did not merely startle him; they pulled him back toward the attack, and because of that he became even more convinced that he needed to keep watch constantly. The more on guard he stayed, the more the world seemed filled with warnings. At times his wife found him sitting rigidly by the window, listening for noise in the street, as if vigilance itself could prevent another disaster.

This pattern had worn him down by the time he sought help. He remained proud of the work he had done for refugees, but he had begun declining assignments that required travel, and his colleagues noticed that he arrived later, spoke less, and left quickly whenever the day involved roads, commotion, or disagreement with another worker. The weight of the self-blame had not eased; if anything, it seemed to make the memory more fixed, more likely to return in flashes and sounds, and those intrusions kept his body braced for danger. He finally came to treatment after his wife told him she was worried by how small his world had become and how tense he was even at home. Minh said he wanted to understand why he could not leave the attack behind, but what frightened him most was the feeling that one loud sound, one contested conversation, or one car ride might pull him back into that day and prove that nowhere outside a few rooms was truly safe.
